cards: Bede was a Northumbrian monk and scholar of the twin monastery of Wearmouth–Jarrow.
Charles Martel was a Frankish military leader and mayor of the palace who effectively ruled the Frankish kingdom in the early eighth century.
Pepin the Short was the son of Charles Martel and the father of Charlemagne.
Alcuin of York was an English scholar and teacher who joined the court of Charlemagne in the late eighth century.
Pope Leo III was bishop of Rome from 795 to 816.
An Lushan was a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded powerful frontier armies in north-eastern China under the Tang Dynasty.
Pepin of Italy was a son of Charlemagne, born Carloman, who was crowned king of Italy in 781 to rule the conquered Lombard kingdom.
Bilge Qaghan was a ruler of the Second Göktürk Khaganate who consolidated the state in the early eighth century.
Óengus son of Fergus was king of the Picts from 729 to 761 and the most powerful ruler in northern Britain of his time.
Widukind was a Westphalian nobleman who led Saxon resistance to Charlemagne in the Saxon Wars.
Saint Boniface was an English monk, born Winfrid, who led the papal mission to the Germans.
Pope Stephen II reigned from 752 to 757.
Abu Muslim was the Persian revolutionary leader who organised the Abbasid movement in Khurasan and led the uprising against the Umayyad Caliphate.
Andal was a Tamil poet-saint, probably of the 8th century, and the only woman among the twelve Alvars, the saints devoted to Vishnu in the Bhakti movement.
Muhammad ibn Qasim was an Umayyad general who conquered Sind in the lower Indus valley around 711 to 712.
Desiderius was the last king of the Lombards in Italy.
Paul the Deacon was a Benedictine monk and historian from a noble Lombard family of Friuli, educated at the royal court of Pavia.
Pelagius was a Visigothic nobleman who founded the Kingdom of Asturias, ruling from about 718 until 737.
Tariq ibn Ziyad was a Berber commander in the service of the Umayyad Caliphate who led the Muslim invasion of the Iberian Peninsula in 711 CE.

Theophanes the Confessor was a Byzantine monk and chronicler whose Chronographia covers the history of the empire from 284 to 813.
Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, often called 18 Rabbit, was the thirteenth king of the Maya city of Copán.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was the Umayyad governor of al-Andalus in 721 and again from 730.
Bappa Rawal is the legendary founder of the power of the Guhila dynasty in Mewar, said in dynastic tradition to have taken the fort of Chittor from its Mori rulers in the early eighth century.
Bögü Qaghan was ruler of the Uyghur Khaganate from 759 to 779.
Corbinian was a Frankish missionary bishop who worked at Freising in Bavaria around 720 and is regarded as the founder of its diocese.
Emperor Xuanzong was an emperor of the Tang Dynasty (r. 713–741) whose era is remembered as a cultural and political high point.
Jasaw Chan K'awiil I was the ruler of the Maya city of Tikal, in modern Guatemala, from 682 to about 734.
Paolo Lucio Anafesto is, according to Venetian tradition, the first Doge of Venice, elected in 697 by the lagoon communities under Byzantine overlordship.
Trisong Detsen was emperor of Tibet from 755 to about 797, the second of the three great 'religious kings' of the Tibetan Empire.
William of Gellone was a Frankish noble and kinsman of Charlemagne who became count of Toulouse around 790.
Willibald was an Anglo-Saxon monk and pilgrim, a kinsman of Saint Boniface.
Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah was the first caliph of the Abbasid Caliphate, reigning from 750 to 754.
Constantine VI (771–c. 797) was Byzantine emperor from 780 to 797, at first under the regency of his mother Irene.
Elisedd ap Gwylog was a king of Powys in the first half of the 8th century.
Ermesinda was a daughter of Pelagius, founder of the Kingdom of Asturias.
Ine of Wessex was king of the West Saxons from 688 to 726, one of the strongest Anglo-Saxon rulers before Alfred.
Kul Tigin was a prince and military commander of the Second Turkic Khaganate, brother of the ruler Bilge Khagan.
Lebuin was an English monk and missionary who worked in the eastern Netherlands in the mid-eighth century, founding a church at Deventer.
Orso Ipato was the third Doge of Venice in tradition but the first whose existence is securely attested, elected in 726 by the lagoon communities during the Iconoclast disputes.
